title: 579. Discrete Mathematics, Counting & Graph Theory: Adjacency Lists
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Describe what the adjacency list of a vertex contains.
questions.question: In an adjacency-list representation of a graph, what does the list of a vertex \(v\) contain?
questions.explanation: Each vertex has its own list, and the list names exactly the neighbours of that vertex. Vertices that are not adjacent to \(v\) are simply absent from its list. In this way every edge is recorded without storing the non-edges.
questions.hint: The representation stores the edges, vertex by vertex.

questions.learningObjective: Find the number of edges of an undirected graph from its adjacency lists.
questions.question: An undirected graph has the adjacency lists \(A\): \(B,C\); \(B\): \(A\); \(C\): \(A,D\); \(D\): \(C\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: The lists have \(2+1+2+1=6\) entries in total. Each edge appears in two lists, once for each endpoint, so the number of edges is \(\dfrac{6}{2}=3\); they are \(AB\), \(AC\), and \(CD\). Taking \(6\) as the number of edges counts every edge twice.
questions.hint: Each edge is written down twice, once at each end.

questions.learningObjective: Read the degree of a vertex from its adjacency list.
questions.question: An undirected graph has the adjacency lists \(P\): \(Q,R,S\); \(Q\): \(P,R\); \(R\): \(P,Q\); \(S\): \(P\). What is the degree of \(P\)?
questions.explanation: The degree of a vertex is the number of its neighbours, which is the length of its adjacency list. The list of \(P\) has the three entries \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\), so the degree is \(3\). The value \(2\) is the degree of \(Q\) and of \(R\).
questions.hint: Count the entries in the list of \(P\).

questions.learningObjective: Check whether adjacency lists can describe an undirected graph.
questions.question: Someone proposes the adjacency lists \(A\): \(B,C\); \(B\): \(A\); \(C\): \(B\) for an undirected graph. Are these lists consistent?

options.label: A
options.text: No; \(C\) is in the list of \(A\), but \(A\) is not in the list of \(C\).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; every vertex has a list, and no vertex is listed twice in one list.

questions.explanation: In an undirected graph adjacency is mutual, so whenever \(y\) appears in the list of \(x\), also \(x\) must appear in the list of \(y\). Here \(C\) is listed under \(A\) but \(A\) is not listed under \(C\); also \(B\) is listed under \(C\) but \(C\) is not listed under \(B\). So the lists cannot come from an undirected graph.
questions.hint: For every entry, check that the reverse entry is present as well.

questions.learningObjective: Find the total length of the adjacency lists of an undirected graph.
questions.question: An undirected graph without loops has \(9\) edges. What is the total number of entries in all its adjacency lists?
questions.explanation: Each edge joining \(u\) and \(v\) contributes two entries: \(v\) in the list of \(u\), and \(u\) in the list of \(v\). So \(9\) edges give \(2\cdot 9=18\) entries. One entry per edge would be correct only for a directed graph that stores out-neighbours.
questions.hint: Count how many list entries a single edge produces.

questions.learningObjective: Find an in-degree from the out-neighbour lists of a directed graph.
questions.question: A directed graph is stored by out-neighbour lists: \(A\): \(B,C\); \(B\): \(C\); \(C\): empty. How many arcs enter \(C\)?
questions.explanation: An arc enters \(C\) whenever \(C\) appears in the list of some vertex. \(C\) appears in the lists of \(A\) and of \(B\), so two arcs enter it. The empty list of \(C\) shows only that no arc leaves \(C\).
questions.hint: Count how often \(C\) appears in the lists of the other vertices.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the sizes of two representations of a sparse graph.
questions.question: An undirected graph has \(1000\) vertices and \(2000\) edges. How do its adjacency matrix and its adjacency lists compare in size?

options.label: A
options.text: The matrix has \(1000000\) entries; the lists have \(4000\) entries in total.

options.label: B
options.text: The matrix has \(2000\) entries; the lists have \(1000000\) entries in total.

questions.explanation: The matrix has one entry for every ordered pair of vertices, \(1000\cdot 1000=1000000\), whatever the number of edges. The lists hold two entries for each edge, \(2\cdot 2000=4000\). For a graph with few edges compared with the number of pairs of vertices, lists need far less space.
questions.hint: The size of the matrix depends only on the number of vertices.

questions.concept: From lists to a matrix row
questions.learningObjective: Convert an adjacency list into a row of the adjacency matrix.
questions.question: An undirected graph on the vertices \(1,2,3,4\) has the adjacency lists \(1\): \(2,4\); \(2\): \(1,3\); \(3\): \(2,4\); \(4\): \(1,3\). In the adjacency matrix, with rows and columns in the order \(1,2,3,4\), what is the row of vertex \(3\)?
questions.explanation: The list of vertex \(3\) names \(2\) and \(4\), so its row has \(1\) in columns \(2\) and \(4\), and \(0\) in columns \(1\) and \(3\). The row \((1,0,1,0)\) belongs to vertices \(2\) and \(4\), whose neighbours are \(1\) and \(3\).
questions.hint: Put \(1\) in the columns of the vertices named in the list of vertex \(3\).

questions.learningObjective: Count the list entries examined in an adjacency test.
questions.question: A vertex \(u\) has degree \(7\), and its adjacency list is not sorted. To decide whether \(u\) is adjacent to a given vertex \(v\), the list of \(u\) is scanned from the beginning. In the worst case, how many entries are examined?
questions.explanation: If \(v\) is the last entry of the list, or is not in the list at all, every one of the \(7\) entries has to be examined. A single look-up suffices for an adjacency matrix, where the answer is the entry in row \(u\), column \(v\), but not for an unsorted list.
questions.hint: Consider the case in which \(v\) is not a neighbour of \(u\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the number of connected components from adjacency lists.
questions.question: An undirected graph has the adjacency lists \(1\): \(2,3\); \(2\): \(1,3\); \(3\): \(1,2\); \(4\): \(5\); \(5\): \(4\). How many connected components does it have?
questions.explanation: Starting from vertex \(1\), the lists lead to \(2\) and \(3\) and to no other vertex, so \(\{1,2,3\}\) is one component. The vertices \(4\) and \(5\) are joined to each other only, forming a second component. No list links the two groups, so the graph is not connected.
questions.hint: Start at vertex \(1\) and follow the lists; see which vertices are never reached.
